answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 70–19 BC · Roman poet, author of the Aeneid
answer.sourceLine: From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book V (line 231), describing the boat race at the funeral games of Anchises: “hos successus alit: possunt, quia posse videntur.” The exact English wording is John Conington’s 1866 verse translation ↗ — a legitimate rendering, though a loose one: the Latin videntur means ‘they seem’ or ‘they appear (able),’ not ‘they think.’

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Those blush to lose a conquering game, / And fain would peril life for fame: / These bring success their zeal to fan; / They can because they think they can.
trail: The Latin original — “hos successus alit: possunt, quia posse videntur”, Aeneid V.229–231 — is documented in the Dickinson College Commentaries ↗.
The exact English wording appears verbatim in John Conington’s 1866 verse translation ↗ and is credited to Conington by Wikiquote ↗.
Earlier translators rendered the line differently — Dryden (1697) wrote “For they can conquer, who believe they can” — per the WIST translation record ↗.
source.excerptNote: Conington’s 1866 verse rendering of Aeneid V.229–231. The famous one-liner translates the final half-line, “possunt, quia posse videntur.”
source.rightsNote: The exact English wording is John Conington’s 1866 verse translation, first published well before 1931 and long out of copyright; the underlying Latin is ancient and public domain. Both are freely reproduced on Wikisource ↗.

author.bio: Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BC) was Rome’s foremost poet, author of the Eclogues, the Georgics, and the epic Aeneid. The line lives in Book V, in the ship race at the funeral games for Aeneas’s father Anchises, where the momentum of belief carries the trailing crews forward. Virgil left the Aeneid unfinished at his death and reportedly asked that it be burned; the emperor Augustus overruled him.

misattribution.heading: Real Virgil, looser English
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Virgil is correct — this really is a line of the Aeneid. The catch is the English: the crisp motivational one-liner is a specific translator’s interpretive phrasing, not a literal rendering of the Latin, and it is almost always quoted without that context.

items.why: The exact English ‘They can because they think they can’ is Conington’s Victorian verse rendering, confirmed on Wikisource ↗. Virgil wrote Latin; the English belongs to his translator.

The Latin verb videntur means ‘they seem’ or ‘they appear (able)’ — a more literal reading is ‘they can because they seem able,’ as the Dickinson commentary ↗ glosses. Conington’s ‘think’ shifts the emphasis from outward appearance to inner belief.
The same half-line has been Englished many ways; Dryden’s famous 1697 version reads ‘For they can conquer, who believe they can,’ per the WIST record ↗. No single ‘official’ wording exists.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Virgil (Aeneid V.231), but the famous English sentence is John Conington’s 1866 translation ↗ — a legitimate rendering that reads ‘think’ where the Latin says ‘seem.’

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The line comes not from a battlefield or a philosopher’s treatise but from a boat race. In Book V of the Aeneid, the crews competing at the funeral games of Anchises are trailing, and Virgil observes that success itself feeds them: they can, because they seem able to. It is a compact psychological insight into momentum and self-belief.

Stripped of its nautical setting and smoothed into ‘They can because they think they can,’ the half-line became a staple of motivational posters, coaching talks, and self-help books — usually with no hint that the memorable English is a Victorian translator’s art laid over Virgil’s Latin.
detailsBody: Hos successus alit: possunt, quia posse videntur — ‘Success nourishes them: they are able, because they appear (to themselves and others) to be able.’ The verb videntur is the passive of videre, ‘to see’ — hence ‘are seen / seem / appear,’ not ‘think.’
context.pull: Success feeds them: they can, because they seem able to.
